title: From 1555 to 1870, Rome’s Jews were walled into 3 hectares by the Tiber
body: Jews have lived in Rome since at least 161 BC, one of the oldest communities in Europe. In July 1555 Pope Paul IV’s bull *Cum nimis absurdum* forced them into a walled quarter of about 3 hectares on the low bank of the Tiber, beside the ruins of the [Portico of Octavia](https://www.turismoroma.it/en/node/1113), which Emperor Augustus had rebuilt in 27–23 BC for his sister. Its gates were locked at night; outside, men had to wear a yellow hat and women a yellow kerchief, and Jews could not own property. The walls did not move, but the people grew in number, from about 2,000 in 1555 to 4,000 by 1656, **over 1,300 a hectare**, so houses rose floor on floor over dark lanes, and the river flooded them. The ghetto ended when Italy took Rome in 1870; its walls came down in 1888, and the Great Synagogue opened on the cleared riverbank in 1904. On 16 October 1943 German police seized 1,259 people in Rome; more than 1,000 were deported to Auschwitz, and only 16 came back. Brass stumbling stones, *pietre d’inciampo*, now mark the last homes of the deported.

slides.question: Rome’s ghetto, walled in by Pope Paul IV in 1555, covered about 3 hectares. About how many people lived in it by 1656?
slides.explanation: About 4,000, twice the 2,000 of 1555: over 1,300 a hectare. Rome today has about 21 people a hectare.

slides.alt: Animation on an evening plan of Rome's ghetto by the Tiber: its walls of 1555 beside the Portico of Octavia; dots for its people filling 3 hectares; houses growing floor by floor; a flood; the walls gone and the Great Synagogue built; a quiet street at dawn with brass stumbling stones.

slides.prompt: In 1555, one floor over the whole quarter would have given each person 15 m². Pick 1656 and add floors until everyone has that much room again.
slides.takeaway: 4,000 people on the same 3 hectares need two floors for the room 2,000 had on one. With walls that never moved, the ghetto could only grow upward.

slides.alt: Photo of the ruined entrance porch of the Portico of Octavia in Rome: a brick arch inside a stone front with two fluted marble columns and a broken triangular pediment, with apartment houses around it and part of a dome at the right edge.
slides.caption: The Portico of Octavia today: mostly Emperor Septimius Severus’s rebuilding of AD 203; the brick arch replaced two columns after an earthquake in AD 442.
slides.credit: Jensens, retouched by Ptyx · Public domain

slides.heading: 16 October 1943
slides.text: German police seized 1,259 people in Rome, 207 of them children, many in and around the old ghetto. After some were released, 1,023 were deported to Auschwitz on 18 October; 15 men and one woman came back. Many others escaped arrest by hiding, often in Catholic institutions.

events.text: First record of Jews in Rome.
Pope Paul IV creates the ghetto.
The ghetto ends as Italy takes Rome.

slides.question: Why did the houses of Rome’s ghetto, walled in by Pope Paul IV in 1555, grow so tall?
options: Its walls stopped it spreading out
Tall houses kept out the floods
slides.explanation: The quarter stayed at about 3 hectares while its people doubled, from about 2,000 in 1555 to 4,000 by 1656, so new room could only be added on top.
